claims.text: Enhanced dynamic mechanical behavior in HEAs arises primarily from locally heterogeneous lattice distortions.
Locally heterogeneous lattice distortions promote simultaneous activation of multiple slip systems under dynamic loading.
Activation of multiple slip systems delays localized failure and permits a combination of strength and ductility.
Homogenization after arc melting ensures a uniform microstructure in the equiatomic single-phase FCC HEA.
Atomic-size misfits among constituent elements produce spatial variations in lattice strain.
Spatial variations in lattice strain create a distribution of local yielding thresholds.
A distribution of local yielding thresholds facilitates staggered and spatially distributed dislocation activation.
Regions with different local yield strengths activate multiple slip systems over a broader strain range.
Reduced strain localization enhances both strength and ductility relative to conventional alloys.
At high strain rates around 10^3 s^-1, the HEA will have higher dynamic yield strength than the conventional-alloy baseline.
At high strain rates around 10^3 s^-1, the HEA will have greater energy absorption and later failure than the conventional-alloy baseline.
Lower atomic-size mismatch in the conventional baseline produces lower lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism should hold for single-phase HEAs with significant lattice-distortion effects, including equiatomic FCC compositions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys or alloys whose dynamic response is dominated by grain-boundary strengthening or precipitation hardening.
Dynamic strain aging and microstructural heterogeneities unrelated to lattice distortion may also contribute to HEA dynamic properties.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in both dynamic yield strength and ductility, or observation of similar or worse strain localization, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
